title: Musk urges top AI labs, Chinese companies to test each other's models
content:
Elon Musk called for the top artificial intelligence companies to work together and test each other's models before they're released to the public, as some of the industry's leaders warn of the technology's dangers and push for greater government regulation.
Speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday, the SpaceX CEO said SpaceX's xAI business, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and "three or four of the leading Chinese companies" should let rivals run a "test harness" on their models to evaluate their safety.
"So, you know, instead of grading your own homework, you would at least have competitors grading your homework and raising the alarm if they see concerns," Musk said.
The debate around how to regulate AI has intensified after the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies spent the weekend warning about the technology's harms and called for a slowdown in model development. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman were among the tech leaders who backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's proposal for a slowdown, marking a rare show of unity.
The push from top AI leaders came amid a broader warning about the fate of humanity as AI researchers sounded the alarm last week, sparked by a post from Jacob Coxon, who announced that he quit his job at Anthropic.
Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, wrote that the leading AI labs are "gambling with our lives." Researchers quickly chimed in, with Evan Hubinger, an alignment lead at Anthropic, also backing Coxon's statements.
"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger wrote.
The Trump administration has pushed back on tech leaders' calls for greater limits on AI. President Donald Trump pushed out a flurry of posts on Truth Social on Monday, referring to fears over AI as a "hoax" and a "scam."
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Tuesday that the private sector is the "right place" to address concerns with AI. He said the government continues to monitor the industry and will use "law enforcement when necessary to make sure that the firms are acting responsibly."
Musk said Monday that his peer-review method may not be a perfect solution, but he added, "The odds that you will find issues are dramatically greater."
Musk acknowledged that rival AI labs that compete with xAI, which SpaceX acquired in February, haven't agreed to his proposal. Amodei, in his essay, suggested that AI labs could agree to third-party technology assessments from "embedded evaluators" who would verify safety practices.
Trump has suggested that any attempts to pace the development of AI would give China the upper hand in developing the technology. Amodei echoed those concerns over the weekend, calling it the "toughest dilemma."
A spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry on Monday called AI companies' push for a slowdown "fear mongering," according to an English translation of their remarks published by Reuters.
"What I'm suggesting here is it's a step in the right direction and it's something that we do quickly," Musk said. "I think it's probably something that China would agree to."

report.summary: Musk proposes that leading AI labs and Chinese firms peer-review each other's models via shared safety test harnesses before public release.
report.background: The proposal lands amid escalating AI-safety warnings from lab leaders and researchers. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in frontier model development; OpenAI's Sam Altman and Musk backed him. Former Anthropic/OpenAI employee Jacob Coxon said leading labs are 'gambling with our lives,' and Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger estimated >10% risk AI could kill all humans within a decade. The Trump administration rejects such warnings: President Trump called AI fears a 'hoax' and 'scam,' while NEC Director Kevin Hassett said the private sector is the right venue for safety fixes, with government monitoring and law enforcement as needed. China's Foreign Ministry dismissed slowdown calls as 'fear mongering.' Musk argues competitors, not labs themselves, should grade models, and predicts China would agree.
key_points: Musk wants xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and three or four leading Chinese AI companies to let rivals run a 'test harness' on their models. Instead of labs grading their own homework, competitors would check safety and raise alarms. He admits no rival has agreed, but says the odds of finding problems are much greater.

The call follows intense safety warnings. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed slowing frontier AI, and Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed him. Ex-Anthropic/OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon said labs are 'gambling with our lives'; Anthropic's Evan Hubinger put extinction risk above 10% in the next decade. This rare unity among rivals raised pressure for outside scrutiny.

Washington is split. President Trump called AI fears a 'hoax' and 'scam,' and NEC Director Kevin Hassett said the private sector is the right place to handle safety, with government monitoring and law enforcement if needed. Trump also argues slowing AI could let China pull ahead, a concern Amodei called the 'toughest dilemma.'

China's Foreign Ministry rejected the slowdown push as 'fear mongering.' Musk still predicted China would agree to mutual testing, saying it is a quick step in the right direction. The geopolitical backdrop complicates any global testing regime, because labs compete fiercely and governments distrust one another's motives.

Amodei offered an alternative: third-party assessments by 'embedded evaluators' who verify safety practices inside labs. Musk's peer-review idea is voluntary and imperfect, but he argues it would surface issues sooner. No major lab has publicly signed on, so the proposal remains a talking point rather than a concrete framework.
report.impact: If adopted, Musk's proposal could normalise pre-release, cross-company safety audits, turning model evaluations into a competitive requirement rather than a self-reported benchmark. For AI developers, it implies more third-party test harnesses, standardised red-teaming and potential release delays; startups may struggle to meet enterprise-grade audit demands. For regular users, the upside is safer, more transparent models, but voluntary peer review may offer weak guarantees, especially amid US-China rivalry and Trump administration deregulation. The bigger signal is that even rivals now publicly acknowledge catastrophic risk, making safety testing a boardroom and policy issue, not just a research niche. Without enforcement, however, the plan may remain symbolic.
report.tools: To follow the testing debate, watch open evaluation frameworks: EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness, Stanford CRFM's HELM, MLCommons AI Safety Benchmark, OpenAI Evals, and the UK AI Safety Institute's Inspect. For adversarial testing, Garak and Promptfoo are useful for red-teaming LLMs. These tools show how a shared 'test harness' could work across labs, though no common standard yet exists for frontier-model safety.
